name: Erection problems and seeing a GP
summary: Erection problems can have physical and psychological causes and may link to heart disease or diabetes, so a GP appointment is worth having if they persist.
keyPoints: Erectile dysfunction means trouble getting or keeping an erection, and the NHS describes it as common.
Causes can be physical, psychological or a mix, and stress, tiredness and alcohol often play a part in occasional problems.
NICE says erection problems share risk factors with heart disease and can be an early sign of it, and diabetes is another link.
The NHS advises seeing a GP or sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for an erection lasting more than 3 to 4 hours, or for sudden chest pain that does not go away.
The MHRA warns that erection pills bought from unregulated online sellers may contain no active ingredient or hidden drugs.

body.heading: What counts as an erection problem?
body.body:
Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, means having trouble getting or keeping an erection. The NHS lists being unable to get an erection, and being unable to keep one long enough to have sex, as the main signs. A lower sex drive can come with it too.

Many men have an off night now and then, and the NHS describes erection problems as common. What matters is whether the problem keeps happening, because that is when the NHS suggests getting help.

body.heading: What causes erection problems?
body.body:
Occasional problems are usually linked to things like stress, tiredness, drinking too much alcohol or using drugs. When problems keep coming back, a physical cause becomes more likely. The NHS names diabetes, operations on the bowel, bladder or prostate, and low testosterone among them. Some medicines can also play a part.

Sexual health services describe causes that are physical, psychological or a mix of both, with anxiety, depression and relationship problems given as examples of the psychological kind.

body.heading: Is there a link with heart disease and diabetes?
body.body:
NICE says erectile dysfunction shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease. It adds that there is growing evidence that it can be an early sign of coronary artery disease and of disease in blood vessels elsewhere in the body. The British Heart Foundation explains that the arteries supplying the penis are narrow, so problems there can be one of the first warning signs of narrowed arteries.

An NHS hospital leaflet on cardiac rehabilitation says erection problems can appear before angina does. Diabetes is another link, since erection problems may be the first sign of diabetes or may develop years after diagnosis. This is a main reason a GP looks at your general health and not only at the erection itself.

body.heading: When should I see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP or a sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening. NHS inform Scotland suggests getting in touch if the problem has lasted more than a few months, things you can do yourself have not helped, and you are bothered by it. A routine GP appointment is the usual route. It is worth telling the GP if you have a heart condition or take nitrate tablets, because one NHS leaflet says people on regular nitrate medicines must avoid some erection treatments and a GP can check this first.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an erection lasts more than 3 to 4 hours. For sudden chest pain that does not go away, or pain spreading to the arm, neck, jaw or back, NHS guidance says to call 999. A hospital leaflet says chest pain that comes and goes is a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: What will the GP ask or check?
body.body: The NHS says the doctor or nurse may ask about your lifestyle and your relationships. They may also carry out health checks, such as taking your blood pressure, and examine your genitals. Depending on what they find, they may refer you for further tests.

body.heading: What treatments are there?
body.body:
Treatment is usually described as a step-by-step approach. Lifestyle changes are the usual starting point, and one NHS trust lists a healthy weight, stopping smoking, regular exercise, less alcohol and less stress. Counselling or talking therapy may help with stress and anxiety, and some sexual health services offer psychosexual therapy.

Tablets are the usual first medicine, according to NHS trusts, and a GP or pharmacist can say whether they suit you. Vacuum pumps are a device that works without medicines and are often offered after tablets. Some NHS areas supply them only to men who meet set criteria, so many men buy their own. Injections, a cream and, for men who do not respond to other treatments, a surgical implant are further options. What is funded differs between local NHS areas, so a GP can explain what is available near you.

body.heading: What about buying erection medicines online?
body.body: The MHRA, which regulates medicines in the UK, warns against buying erection pills from unregulated websites, social media or messaging apps. It says such products may contain no active ingredient, the wrong amount, hidden drugs or toxic ingredients. It adds that the risks are higher for people with heart disease or high blood pressure, or who take other medicines. The MHRA advises using only UK-registered pharmacies, and online pharmacies in Great Britain can be checked on the General Pharmaceutical Council website. Suspicious medicines or websites can be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.
